core: Collaboration platforms are digital tools that let multiple people work together on shared content, in four main categories: real-time co-editing of shared documents, team chat/messaging, video conferencing/meetings, and shared task/project boards
Real-time co-authoring lets several people edit the same file at once, showing each collaborator's presence and their changes live
Version history records past versions of a file (who changed what and when) and lets a user restore or copy an earlier version
Synchronous collaboration means participants take part at the same time; asynchronous collaboration does not require them to be present simultaneously
Team chat organizes conversation into channels (topic- or team-scoped) versus one-on-one and group direct messages
Task/project boards visualize work as cards that move across columns (e.g., To Do, In Progress, Done) to track progress
Sharing uses tiered permissions (view vs comment vs edit) and carries a security and privacy responsibility
supporting: Presence indicators (flags/live cursors) show who is in a document and where they are working
Named versions and restore-to-previous-version behavior in version history
Standard channels are open to all team members and searchable; private channels are limited to invited people
Access controls for meetings: passwords/access codes, waiting rooms, locking a meeting, admitting and removing attendees
Sharing with specific people (by address) versus anyone with the link
outOfScope: Cloud storage and file-sync mechanics (owned by Cloud Storage; referenced only as where shared files live)
Email as a messaging channel (owned by Email Basics)
Document editing/formatting features themselves (owned by Word Processing)
Privacy law, data-collection trade-offs, and individual privacy strategy (owned by Privacy)

claims.claim: Collaboration platforms are digital tools that let people work together on shared content, spanning four main categories: real-time co-editing of shared documents, team chat/messaging, video conferencing, and shared task/project boards.
Real-time co-authoring lets several people edit the same document at the same time, and each editor can see the presence of others and the changes they are making as they happen.

Co-authoring depends on the file being stored in a shared online location; without real-time collaboration a user can still edit at the same time as others but must save periodically to send and see changes.
Version history records past versions of a file, showing who changed what and when, and lets a user restore an earlier version or copy it; users can also name specific versions.

Synchronous communication happens when all parties take part in the exchange at the same time (live meetings, conference and video calls, instant messaging), while asynchronous communication does not require the parties to be present simultaneously (email, project blogs, recorded messages).

Team chat organizes conversation into channels where messages are shared with a whole team, distinct from one-on-one or group direct messages; standard channels are open to and searchable by all team members, while private channels are visible only to invited people.

Sharing permissions are tiered roles: a Viewer can view and download, a Commenter can additionally comment, and an Editor can change the content and share it; the owner controls permissions. Files can be shared with specific named people or with anyone who has the link.

A task/project (kanban) board is a visual tool that represents work as cards arranged in columns such as To Do, In Progress, and Done, helping a team visualize workflow, limit work in progress, and identify bottlenecks.

Sharing and online collaboration widen the attack surface, so securing collaboration means controlling access (access codes/passwords, waiting rooms, locking meetings, admitting and removing attendees), limiting file and screen sharing, managing recordings, and keeping applications updated.
Good sharing practice is to grant the least access needed for the task, invite only the intended people rather than disseminating links widely, and periodically review who has access.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft was placeholder boilerplate ('Collaboration Platforms is a foundational concept in Computer Literacy. This lesson introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it.') with no verifiable substance. All of it was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced placeholder text with sourced definitions of the four platform categories and the cross-cutting concepts (synchronous vs asynchronous, version history, permissions).

Added the co-authoring presence/live-change mechanic and the cloud-storage prerequisite, the tiered view/comment/edit permission model, and the CISA-based security responsibilities of sharing, none of which the draft mentioned.
Handed storage/sync to Cloud Storage, email to Email Basics, document formatting to Word Processing, and privacy trade-offs/law to Privacy, per anti-duplication guidance.
rightsIssues: Microsoft Support, Google Help, and Atlassian pages are copyrighted; used REFERENCE_ONLY with original prose only. The Kirkwood Project Management Basics OER is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (NonCommercial), so it was treated as reference-only and its wording was not reproduced. The CISA video-conferencing guidance is a U.S. federal government work (public domain); facts were still synthesized in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: Collaborate on Word documents with real-time co-authoring
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: several people can work in the same document and, if others are working on it, you see their presence and the changes they are making; real-time collaboration requires a current app/subscription, and without it you can still edit simultaneously but must save from time to time to exchange changes; the shared document opens from a link in the browser, i.e. it lives in a shared online location. Reference-only; prose written independently.

sourceRecords.title: See changes in your Google Docs, Sheets & Slides (version history)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: version history shows earlier versions of a file and who changed what; users can open a previous version and 'Restore this version', or make a copy; users can create named versions; editing permission is needed to browse history. Used for the version-history/restore claim. Reference-only; original wording used.

sourceRecords.title: Share files from Google Drive (Viewer, Commenter, Editor)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the tiered roles: Viewer (view and download), Commenter (view, comment, download), Editor (edit, share, download); Owner controls all permissions. Also supports sharing with specific people by email versus making a file available to anyone with the link. Used for the permissions/sharing model. Reference-only; original wording used.

sourceRecords.title: Guidance for Securing Video Conferencing
sourceRecords.notes: U.S. federal government work (public domain). Four principles: connect securely; control access (require an access code/password, manage who can attend, enable waiting rooms to vet attendees, lock the event once everyone has joined, be able to admit and remove attendees, be cautious disseminating invitation links); manage file and screen sharing and recordings (limit sharing to trusted sources, limit file types, make participants aware of recording); update to the latest versions. PDF (CISA_Guidance_for_Securing_Video_Conferencing_S508C.pdf) read via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-19 after the site returned 403 to the fetcher. Used for the security-responsibility-of-sharing claims; facts synthesized in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Types of Communication (Project Management Basics, 8.3)
sourceRecords.notes: Open textbook. Defines synchronous communication as all parties taking part at the same time (live meeting, conference/audio/video call, computer-assisted conference with a jointly edited document, instant messaging, texting) and asynchronous communication as not requiring parties to be present at the same time (mail, fax, email, project blog). License CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 confirmed in page footer; NonCommercial, so treated as reference-only. Page read via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-19 after a 403 to the fetcher. Facts synthesized; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Teams and channels in Microsoft Teams
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: channels are where a team's conversations, files, and apps are shared with the whole team; a standard channel is open to all team members and its posts are searchable by others; a private channel is limited to invited people; distinct from one-on-one or group chats. Used for the channels-vs-direct-messages distinction. Reference-only; original wording used.

sourceRecords.title: What is a kanban board?
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: a kanban board is a visual project-management tool that uses cards, columns, and work-in-progress limits to visualize tasks, manage workflow, and identify bottlenecks; a basic board has columns such as To Do, In Progress, and Done, and cards represent individual work items. Page read via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-19 after a 403 to the fetcher. Used for the task/project-board category. Reference-only; original wording used.
